title: I have a lambda
content:
The inevitable happened. We're even counting the years since. We're in calm waters, not a single wave in the sea. But... at least one of you would swim towards me ;_;

I tripled my carbon footprint overnight.
Imagine a future where you can actually get cold in winter. Your friends invite you out, and you have to wear a coat. You never, ever take a minibus. Istanbul's public transport card doesn't require ID verification. Everyone you meet looks amazing. You get together once a week to play D&D 3.5, and the whole world hates everything new along with you. Dreaming is free, after all.
It's rare for me to run out of things to say. When it comes to rambling on, nobody's better than me. But lately, I've been surrounded by some pretty stupid people. People whose lack of understanding isn't evident in their answers, but in their faces. If they were trying, great. But they give up from the start.
I've stopped expecting anyone to teach me anything; I can't teach anyone myself. Years of accumulated knowledge are gathering dust on a bookshelf, like a Turkish book whose origin is unknown. I really want to be useful. Whatever happens, I want my existence to lead to something.

My crimes always went unpunished; I wish you could have taken some of them with you.
I'd understand if they didn't like me. They're so eager to see me. But when we sit across from each other, they just listen in silence. I don't know, I don't really remember what it used to be, but it seems like things used to be more interactive. When I ask a question, they just stare at me and freeze. I have to say ten sentences just to get one from them. And the answers I get seem to come from somewhere memorized.
I find myself explaining very simple things at length, for example. It spoils my enjoyment.
When I talk to someone, it's like we're showing each other picture cards. Whatever the word evokes, that's what it is. If I say something a little complicated, I regret it. If I knew better, I wouldn't lift my head from my games. Why am I paying the price for their ignorance?

I will sleep when I die.
"You're with the wrong people." Are there even any people left?
I barely have a handful, and I tolerate them by making huge compromises. Their words and actions don't match, and they can't even spend two minutes brainstorming. I'm so fed up with people. I don't understand how they manage to agree with the rest of the world on everything. At least try to add some color to the conversation. Let's explore a couple of hypothetical scenarios together. But no, they're boring even in their fantasies.
I read somewhere that people with below-average IQs can't grasp hypothetical scenarios very well. They can't go beyond the scenario, even in their fantasies. I wish we saw this consistency in more important matters.
I tried to sabotage my life for a long time because I was so bored. Literally everything I did backfired. I kept doing what I was doing, and they kept praising me. I guess they don't even understand what I'm saying; they judge my actions by the air I give off. If I acted even slightly shy, they'd walk all over me.

I'm quadrupling my carbon footprint!
I'm trying to be positive now; maybe it really isn't my fault. Maybe I'm paying the price for being a shitty person, not for reading too many books in high school.
Still, let's be realistic. Even if I were playing a different role, it still leads to the same place. It's not a cultural divide, because I don't have that kind of intellectual side. I just want a reason to step outside the house. How can there really be nothing to do in this huge city of Istanbul? How can all the activities consist of sitting in a place and drinking? I went to places that are supposed to be teeming with nerds a few times. Even there, I didn't hear anything new. It's like someone pressed the stop button on the world and flushed it.

We need to kiss sometimes too.
I don't know if it's just me, but conversations don't last long anymore unless you're actively trying to hook up with someone. To play an MMORPG with someone and have a voice call, I have to trick them with my dick. I even had to build a harem just to play D&D.
I don't know. My expectations were so different. I thought new things would test me, challenge me a bit. Life would get more complicated, and so on. Instead, I've faced a huge drop in quality. It's like there's no material left; I'm just stuck with cheap repetitions. I can't even find solace in hedonism anymore.

We've whined enough.
Thank you for reading my personal blog.

title: things stolen from me
content:
Let's cut down this huge tree and count the rings inside.

Let's cut down this huge tree and count the rings inside.
I need to talk a little about things I got away with. After all, I have a Legacy to keep alive. Otherwise, what difference would there be between me and you?
There's no need to start from the beginning of time. I'll continue from where I left off so that no one gets confused.
I categorize the players in my life according to their ability to dominate their surroundings. I carefully observe how lasting their words and actions are, and how much they deviate from the course our world is following. If this deviation remains below three degrees, I can overlook it based on certain invisible constants.

I'll start with my first victim.
I never attempted to burden myself with the mission of a prophet. The path I try to follow in my life is more like that of a dervish. Time and space are no longer relevant. There is no destination. Whoever wants something from me takes it, but dervishes carry axes. They carry these axes so that if a wild animal appears before them, they can strike it on the head. In short, I may be aimless, but I am still sharp-witted.
Sometimes, instead of an animal, a tree appears before me. This tree asks me to prune it. Although I don't want to waste my axe like this, I can't refuse it. I start with the drooping branches, and when those branches recede and clear my path, I prune the rotten branches. These branches, shaped by the strong winds the tree withstands, wrap around the tree's trunk. They surround it like armor. Because I can't wield the axe skillfully, sometimes I miss the branches and wound the tree itself.
Actually, this is the job of a gardener. But this creature in need of help can only be found by me because I stray from the path and delve into the bushes. I know that if I'm not the one to prune it, nobody else will.

If a tree falls by itself in a deserted forest...
I thought repetition was my curse. Things we inherited from Sisyphus. No, repetition was a warning. Repetition is the point where the unstoppable force strikes that object, which is perfectly manageable and will never move. Someone important once said; You go around the wall, I get up every time I fall and run back to it until I knock the wall down with my head. That man, one day, decided to walk around the wall, but for some reason, he put me in its place. Here, rather than Sisyphus, we became Heracles, bearing the weight of Atlas.
You can't move anywhere when you have the weight of the whole world on your shoulders. You understand. Now that we've vomited out cheap symbolism from our system, let's get to the point. The burden I carried was my loved ones, who would never learn. They hadn't come into existence on their own; their parents had created them. They were helpless against them. They either became like them or walked the path they had drawn. In return, I stood by the side of the road, waving to them. They really wanted to come to me. But for that, they needed to think for themselves, to leave their comfort zones.
As I showed some of them the path to freedom, the increasing risk made them more cowardly. They became so cowardly that the first thing they took refuge in was the system society had already imposed on them. Like a child who falls off a bicycle and hesitates to ride it again, the fault wasn't in their own incompetence, but in the methods. And who knows how many times I fell before I could prove that these methods worked.
It wasn't my cult leader charisma that inspired them. It was my approachability. I hadn't descended from the top of a special caste system. In fact, I was right on the ground. My story wasn't a success story. It was a harbinger of a happy ending that could be reached at some point. We hadn't reached it yet, but we were very close.

Ta-da! Actually, there was a spoon, I just wasn't sharing it with you.
My disgust is directed at those who are afraid to live. Because they are the ones who most often break their own rules. Because they offer everything that pertains to them to be broken. To be broken by masters, to be broken for alms, to be broken so that they feel good.
This fear stems from a refusal to accept. But this is not a virtue. All that needs to be done is for a person to accept that they are without virtue, without honor, without backbone. Everything that makes us feel like we have character is a fabrication. It makes us invisible to the weapons of society. Conformists are blind, because an unstimulated sense dulls. If one day they stumble, they won't even realize that the power punishing them is the very weapons they have become blind to. The logic of causality is lost. If a person is also foolish, the only resource they can turn to is their own inner world. Delirium begins here. The foundation is already rotten, and every system built on that foundation is crooked.
Faith speaks much of the soul. Yet, it is unknown whether the soul was always immortal.
Humanity should live in the present moment. Not in the afterlife, in imagination, or in assumptions. But we could never make peace with ourselves. We could never accept who we were. Because of our ignorance stemming from our inability to understand the world, all we could decide about what we would become was what they allowed us to be.

Let everyone change their name to Damkina.
I always tried to create a safe space for the people around me. A place where they could be themselves and wouldn't be judged. I simply directed my corners toward the drinks and food they brought from outside. As long as they didn't annoy me, they all got what they wanted.
They thought they deserved it. Yet, behind all this were the struggles I endured. That's what made them special; the fact that they were deemed worthy in my eyes was my sacrifice. But like someone from Istanbul eating a good Iskender kebab for the first time, they thought they could come back here and eat the same kebab again. Life isn't fair. At this point, they will only carry the delusion of an incomplete teaching. Because no one will take them to the right Iskender kebab place, and they will be too shy to ask me.

A bird that flies out of the nest is caught by a cat. Ham.
That's all I could do. I didn't manage to do it right. Some snakes should have their heads crushed early, damn it, I'm a die-hard animal lover. Maybe I don't touch every cat I see and I often have to swing a stick at monkeys, but I sincerely hope you all arrive at your destinations safe and sound.
Singularity, after all, is only granted to freethinkers.

title: If I come to my senses
content:
My mind is in turmoil. The medication I'm taking is having an unwanted effect on me. I'm in conflict with my lifestyle because of it. The source of all my problems is people. This isn't some hard-to-understand secret. When I take the medication, I feel restless and I want to talk. To talk a lot.

Ice-cold, low-calorie energy drinks are my real medicine.
I apologize to all of you for my cryptic introductory posts. I made an explanation for this kind of thing in my previous blog. Normally, I would limit these kinds of vague, nonsensical things to a paragraph or two at the beginning of my posts. This time, it completely overwhelmed me. I haven't written in a long time, that's why I say so.
For those reading my blog for the first time, let me quote from my previous post:
"Among the advice given to writers, there's a saying, 'get rid of the first thousand bad words.' When I talk about the stew I ate and my dream, I'm actually trying to do that a little bit. I need to cleanse myself by draining the bad blood from my system.
Because they poisoned me very badly, my friend, very badly."
I used to keep my blog to myself. Like a diary, I didn't share it with anyone. Whoever found it, found it somehow. Of course, things changed, and later I started sharing, even dragging people into this hobby. Anyway, I never paid attention to what I wrote. But as I heard the comments of those who read my blog, I realized that I was actually creating something interesting, whether I knew it or not.
My nonsensical introductions or extremely vague ramblings. I used to think that someone reading these wouldn't understand them or find them relatable. But apparently, for some people, it's even more valuable. I manage to stimulate their minds without explaining anything. I enjoy hearing things like that.

My cats love the taste the most.
I played Minecraft all night. Finally, I overcame a conditioning that had been holding my mind captive. I couldn't play alone. It's a social game, after all, so naturally, the idea that "This should be played with other people" was ingrained in my mind. I continued until my eyes started to close from sleepiness. I shut off my thoughts and immersed myself in the digital Lego world. The reason I stopped playing was that when I tried to program something impossible with redstone, the gears in my brain started turning again.
I'm good at art. But for a long time – an extremely long time – I haven't been able to create anything new. I can't blame myself, though. I've thought about this a lot and I have some theories.
Art feeds on experience. And I'm not experiencing very interesting things anymore. As a hikikomori, my life is essentially what I experience in my room. All my material comes from the past, but as the years pass, I've naturally become estranged from my memories.
When I look at them, all the works that interest and inspire me share certain common characteristics. Of course they will, but I'm talking about the creative processes here. They never, ever create what they write or draw alone. The creative process takes precedence over the planned story and what will be told. Manga, for example, go through a strong editorial process. A mangaka doesn't do everything alone; they work with a team. While drawing a new chapter each month, the events of that month, the readers' thoughts, and the artist's own self-criticism are all interwoven into the work. I can tell that the dialogues I read weren't written by a man sitting in front of a blank sheet of paper. Yes, I know, these aren't deeply hidden, private pieces of information; I haven't just recently realized this. But lately, I've gained a new perspective and reassembled the pieces.
Most artists aren't satisfied with their work. We can see this especially at the beginning of stories. The form they take according to the industry, the rules they follow in order to create their art, the publishers' demands, the market... Only when they are "successful" do they break free from this and truly express their feelings as they are. The Alien series was the first thing that put this idea in my head.
Film trilogies have a common thread. The FNAF film adaptation, for example, isn't a game series I normally follow. But people are curious about such products of internet culture. I went to see it in theaters because Josh Hutchserson, an actor I like, was in the lead role. The first film was quite weak; perhaps because of the genre, I could see that the production's decisions were quite commercially oriented. Therefore, I didn't approach it critically at all. When I went to see the second film, I realized it was consistent with the theory I'd formed after watching the Alien series. This time, the film was fuller, more entertaining, and more free-flowing. I'm eagerly awaiting the third film.
My theory is this: The first film is always about numbers. It uses formulas strictly to reach as many people as possible and be easily understood. It avoids upsetting the audience. The second film is the real film; the success of the first reveals what they originally intended to do. Once the directors see that the film has already established itself in the audience, and with audience feedback, they begin to open up space for the artists. And that's how the third film happens. There are no longer any boundaries; the mainstream audience might not like it, but the final blow to the series' cult status is struck here. You can analyze any trilogy in this way. Back to the Future's focus on cowboys is entirely an American cinematic metaphor; Alien 3 – if you watch the uncensored director's cut – presents the metaphors the series originally intended to explore in an experimental way. Even in Marvel films I don't particularly like, I've seen the same themes in the Guardians of the Galaxy trilogy and End Game. End Game, in particular, literally transported me into the writers' room. It offered a beautiful critique of clichés and genre conventions. Each character was developed in a way that was seamlessly integrated with their actors. Now they could gain weight, retire, or even pursue stale, easy solutions like time travel without fear or justification.

What saddens me is that I'll never be a part of something like this.
There's a great documentary about how South Park was made. You can watch it on YouTube or something. I highly recommend it. Knowing that people like them exist is really important if you're an artist. Especially after what they did in their later seasons, they broke the bar they were constantly raising. I always see a prejudice against these kinds of series. After all, Rick & Morty has established itself in culture because of its fanbase. Anyway, the reason I'm mentioning this is because you've probably heard why the guys who make Black Mirror don't release new episodes. They say, "What can we do? Everything we've made has become real, are we going to film what's already there?"
South Park is like that too; people keep saying, "Our reality is already a South Park episode." It's always been like that. They're creative comedians, after all, they always manage to twist and turn things and grab hold of them from somewhere. Even though they're quite direct, they hide the subject matter behind a veil of "fiction." Matt and Trey, if you follow them, know that they're extremely dissatisfied with the state of the world. South Park is their call to action for people. But after making twenty seasons of a show, even they can't escape the thought, "South Park is like that." Therefore, the way the final season, which began as if hiding behind layers of fiction, gradually lifted those veils, and the moment the character in question appeared on screen, the complete disbelief built on reality was shattered, was a historic moment.
Fanboyism aside, seeing this triggered a long introspection within myself. My trilogy theory, the whip that South Park lashed at my neck, finally made me realize why everything I did felt so repulsive to me.

My dreams are writing stories for me now.
Artist crises used to be a topic I actively discussed in art communities and fine arts circles. There was something that always bothered me, something that constantly recurred. Leaving aside those who had already established themselves as artists, the others I encountered, amateurs and those just starting out, were always obsessed with how to market their art before even beginning. Strategizing is certainly good, but I don't think I need to explain how harmful it can be for the individual. Even though I consider myself someone who has overcome this, I realized there's another dimension to it.
What influenced me was comics, especially manga. I want to draw manga, I still desperately want to. Yet, what always held me back from starting a proper series was this format, shaped by marketing. The product's constraints. Yes, if you're going to draw manga, you have to follow a certain page format, story structure rules, and visual storytelling techniques. But this is a format entirely shaped by marketing. And it's incredibly restrictive.
I'm working on this these days. I'm reviewing alternatives. And so the idea of making a Visual Novel started to look really appealing.

Of course, things like that take a lot of time.
If I manage to overcome my depression – and I have some things to take care of – I'd like to talk a little bit about my work on Visual Novels. Wish me luck. And of course, if you're interested, you can reach me at the email address on the homepage.
Again, thank you for reading my personal blog.

title: narcissistic abuse
content:
We all have our own ways of coping with life’s stress. Usually, these are things that harm us. Instead of confronting our problems, we look for escape routes. Eating disorders, addictions, dissociation... Things that sound disturbing. Everyone says that escaping or filling the emptiness inside us with these is not virtuous. In my opinion, that’s complete nonsense.

Our flesh to our nails, our lives to our teeth.
The experience of being human is not just about feeling good. Maturity comes from accepting the dark side of life. No one claims not to know this when asked, but who truly lives with the consequences of knowing it? Even if you accept your situation, the rest of the people — the majority — somehow turn you into a part of their own “feel-good” cycles. Let’s not forget, the world consists of people.
When a person turns inward, enemies appear before them. If you’ve researched psychology even a little, you know what kind of entities these are. We will talk about the most dangerous of them: honor, virtue, and ego.
Honor is often confused with pride. We don’t like proud people; we label them as arrogant. But if their pride is justified — more convenient for us — we share in that pride. Sometimes the pride we feel seems like a joke. The reason behind this is also the cornerstone of comedy: taking something no one cares about or that isn’t that important and treating it with excessive seriousness. Good jokes make you think while making you laugh because they offer original ideas and different perspectives by drawing conclusions about topics no one bothers to think about. Still, in the end, pride is feeling good about one’s actions. For most people, the line blurs here.
Among the public, honor is associated with self-respect. This is another misconception. Because self-respect is shaped by the environment and formed through comparison. Values are weighed according to the moral system taken as reference. Honor is not self-respect. On the contrary, it can even lead to the destruction of self-respect. Because honor emerges from remaining loyal to one’s beliefs and displaying a consistent character without compromising them. If necessary, one suffers for it, allows oneself to be crushed, but at the end of the day does not deviate even slightly from one’s path. Self-respect is not completely outside the equation, however; a person can still feel proud for not abandoning their honor. The danger lies here. Because how these values we hold in such high regard emerge may not be entirely within our control.
Being virtuous is considered wise behavior for society. We call a person virtuous if they are defined by the values society and general morality love and exalt. There is no other definition of virtue. Unless morality is restructured, its conditions remain fixed. However, moral systems are always distorted. Utilitarianism lies behind them and they are period-specific. Otherwise, rest assured, this debate would not have continued since the beginning of human history. Although definitions of good and evil are logically based on positive foundations, the moral system in which they are formulated comes with a cultural package. Even if you sit down and determine which values are truly immutable and genuine and which ones are inserted to benefit from the system, the moment you begin to question it, it is seen as an attack on the integrity of the system.

We are on the verge of uncovering the great conspiracy.
In our culture, suffering and impoverished people are always portrayed as virtuous and honorable individuals. Nietzsche already explains the reasons for this in his book.
Because humans are a primate species. Our brains have developed mechanisms to cope with difficult conditions and to be motivated to progress. The way to eliminate these difficult conditions and reach the rewards we desire more easily is to restrict our freedom. For this reason, our non-virtuous human needs are pushed aside. They are called ego and demonized. This is an operation of alienation and separation. What is imposed on us while growing up guides how we form our character later. Thus, what we call virtue forces us to be self-sacrificing for the good of others.
The ego comes into play here. In the conflict between the instincts inherited from our ape ancestors and the system established for the peace of society, this part of our self acts as a mediator. Thanks to it, we can sleep peacefully when we lay our heads on the pillow at night.
The danger lies here. Separating ego or instincts from character elevates morality to a sacred place. Like two liquids that do not mix, one on top and one at the bottom. The situation remains the same: for one to stay on top, it must crush and step on the other. If we reason it out, imagine a glass half dirty water and half clean water; no matter how hard you try, when you attempt to drink from that glass, you will inevitably taste the dirty water too, like the grounds of Turkish coffee.
Because what we call morality is not merely built on instinct; it is created based on instincts. Otherwise, why would we go so far as to restrict the freedom of others? Let’s be realistic: we all have things we would like to erase from the face of the earth simply because we don’t like them. In some cases, these are specific people.
People also fabricate a moral cover for emotions they cannot cope with. For things they do not dare to attempt — perhaps because they fear the consequences, or because they lack the power — they want others to be punished. That is why the most extreme homophobes often have repressed emotions behind them; that is why bullies evoke empathy when you examine the reasons for their behavior. Behind the veil of morality, you will find jealousy, oppression, helplessness, and more.

Nothing human is alien to me.
And thus the snake swallows its own tail. Morality is invented to safeguard what stems from our ego. We feed ourselves, find someone to warm our bed, and live without fear of being robbed. In return, we confine everything that makes us special to the limits society permits. We balance our ego so that honor remains within the equation and structure our character within the definition of virtue. Like fleas in a jar, even when these rigid rules loosen, learned helplessness prevents us from stepping beyond the threshold.
The world created by this makes us feel guilty. To cope with that guilt, we create coping mechanisms. These consist only of what we are allowed to do. Alcohol, drugs, food, sex — we become trapped in a lukewarm, hedonistic cycle. Our choice lies between two options: either to suffer for being ourselves, or to replace the harm caused by being ourselves with habits that disturb no one and cause less damage than we would.
This is the second layer. It remains behind closed doors. Your bedroom or a night at a club. Kept secrets create new problems. A deal is made for freedom, creating the illusion that it is the only place where you can be yourself. That is abuse. The real you, the outside you, the bedroom you, the you with your lover, the you with your friend... You become so fragmented that you cannot even hold anyone accountable for the injustices done to you. Because each part is justified under its own conditions. Where is honor in all of this?

What do we have to hurt besides each other?
Since the end always leads to the same place, since what we do to fill the emptiness inside us determines our final state and causes us suffering; why are we so insistent on continuing this game? If we wrap ourselves in layers only to return to where we started, why not be ourselves from the beginning and suffer for it instead of complicating everything further?
I have already made my decision and I am bearing the consequences. Because I chose to be myself, I remain alone with my honor intact. And ironically, in the end, I am not in a very different place from those who chose the other path. I do not feel as though I have lost anything, nor as though I am missing something. Like everyone else, I have the same things; like everyone else, I am unhappy; like everyone else, I stare at the same things on a screen all day.
My only complaint is this curtain drawn between us. It makes reaching each other difficult. Even while building our “safe” spaces, we fall into the same mistake. All we can do is leave breadcrumbs behind in the hope that our paths might cross with people similar to us.
But it is not only those similar to us who follow these breadcrumbs; the hungry follow them too. Those helpless and identity-less individuals created by the system are not selective. For them, these breadcrumbs we leave only lead to victims they can cling to like leeches. After experiencing this enough times, we begin looking for the fault in ourselves. The people we thought reached us because they understood us disappoint us. A person who cannot even live as themselves — let alone openly — distances themselves when they see that even their breadcrumbs do not lead to good outcomes.
Humanity’s monkey-like nature is at play again; after all, we are animals. When hunters discover where these breadcrumbs lead, they begin leaving false trails that misdirect and trap those who are truly meant to reach you. In the end, no one reaches their intended destination. Witnessing this, when one’s identity is taken and exploited in this way, there remains no option but to hide. One falls into the grip of the established order, accepts defeat, and throws oneself into the gears of the system.

This is not fatalism but Stoicism.
Perhaps at some point we can become part of a culture that truly reaches us. We can have fun for a while until the hungry and the trappers arrive. We have the opportunity to form genuine friendships. Yet once this space is discovered, it degenerates again, absorbed into the system, and everything we dislike flows back into it. If you stay, you remain among those who are there only to benefit; if you chase the next new thing, you leave a large part of your identity behind.
I love lo-fi music. It truly soothes my soul. Everything I mentioned happened to it as well. First, they realized how easily it could be imitated; at least at that time, those who still had some skill could resort to it. Now hours-long playlists are created with the press of a button. All for pocket money.
Things that once defined our identity are now worn like costumes by others.

title: vitamin in the peel
content:
If you could see the future, could you change what is going to happen?
The answer depends on how much control you have over your life. Seeing the future is not a special skill. Look around; everyone, including you, does it. You can more or less predict what might happen tomorrow. If you are an observant person, the future you can predict becomes even more certain, and you can visualize a more distant future in your mind.

Everyone is the conductor of their own orchestra.
What we call science is about establishing a common language. It takes things people find indisputable, subjective, and complex, and turns them into data. Thus, a scientist can process this information without prejudice. Of course, I am excluding the humanities. If we go into that, we will never get out.
The part that concerns us is the deterministic structure of the universe. As you know, the matter that makes up the universe consists of atoms, and atoms consist of smaller subatomic particles. Their arrangements form elements; their reactions and movements are based on the laws of physics. In other words, everything that happens, has happened, and will happen follows these laws. Accordingly, if we possessed knowledge of every substance currently in the universe and the effects acting upon them, we could calculate everything that will occur until the end of the universe. However, we do not even need that much information to predict the end of the universe. The laws of thermodynamics can foresee it with quite limited data.
Machines are constrained possibilities. If a car moves unpredictably no matter where you turn the steering wheel or how hard you press the pedal, and does not do what you want, it is broken. For this not to happen, the wheels must turn in a certain direction, align with the steering wheel, and a certain amount of fuel must be injected into the engine when you press the pedal. The machines we use daily gradually deteriorate with use, yet we continue to use them until they stop functioning completely or begin to produce deviations beyond our tolerance.
A living being is also a machine. In short, the same rules apply to us. The more we know about our bodies, the more control we have. For example, a young girl who knows her menstrual cycle and its phases will experience a tenfold increase in her quality of life compared to before.

Knowing does not always make us capable of doing.
The structure of the universe is deterministic. Everything has a cause and a resulting consequence. Therefore, free will is an illusion. From the moment we are born, our destiny is determined, and it is impossible to change it. This gives rise to existential crises. Some people take refuge in fatalism. Others completely deny that free will is a lie. Yet there is a tried and tested way to cope with this existential distress: Stoicism.
In summary: A person is responsible for what they can control in their life. They must accept what they cannot control. If they understand themselves thoroughly and manage to grasp the causality and logic behind their actions, this grants them awareness of their choices. This becomes a new definition of “free” will. It is still limited, but at least it creates the power to decide among available options. Thus, we can understand the true nature of decisions that appear harmless and avoid them to create a better life.
We constantly encounter this in therapy sessions, personal development, and religious teachings. We are all already familiar with the foundations of Stoicism. But it is also necessary to know what those foundations are built upon, because this system of thought is, again, something that can be manipulated.
Thought systems claiming that human beings and their lives have a purpose and meaning draw heavily from Stoicism. Yet this idea actually originates from Cynicism, from the Cynics. The path to becoming a Cynic is through questioning. It questions the reasons behind human behavior and the social environment it creates.

Sometimes the answer to the problem is hidden within the problem itself.
At one point in the history of philosophy, thinkers were obsessed with defining the simplest description of man. The most widely accepted definition, the one that supposedly ended the debate, is Aristotle’s: “Man is a rational animal.” Yet most people do not know the tragic story behind how we arrived there.
Plato’s first answer to the question “What is man?” was “Man is a two-legged, featherless creature.” Here, feather refers to bird feathers, not hair. Technically, it was correct. Diogenes then appeared holding a plucked chicken and declared, “Behold, a man!” This did not produce a better definition. Plato later maintained his original description, only adding, “Man’s nails are flat.”
Aristotle’s definition was also challenged: “Then is an animal a human who cannot think?” And thus the underlying problem became visible.
Man cannot accept that he is an animal and no different from other animals.
Today we know that using language and reasoning are not exclusive to humans. Some species use their own grammar and syntax. They do not merely communicate with sounds; those sounds lose meaning if not arranged correctly. The Cynics, who do not separate humans from animals, gain relevance once again.

Today as well, we knew a lot and spoke little.
We can reach correct answers, even if our methods are wrong. Until someone proves us wrong, we cling to what we believe is correct. Science operates this way as well; truth remains until disproven. But it is not always that simple. The physics we use to build structures on Earth may fail in space. When neither can replace the other, yet both are correct, what should we do?
If humans are machines—and they are—then society becomes a massive system composed of countless smaller machines. A larger machine. Like our body, it survives through the collective functioning of many smaller organisms. And just as our body contains cells that are not truly “us,” we coexist symbiotically with other entities that do not carry our DNA. Our gut flora alone can rewrite our character if it chooses to.
Our awareness in this context becomes no different from gambling. Even if we foresee what will happen and make our decisions as consciously as possible, there are infinite details we may never know, or may ignore because we cannot comprehend them.
Should all the various paths we take to reach desired outcomes therefore be considered correct? Is reality truly built on such subjective foundations? Should we accept that everyone has their own “truth” and live accordingly?

We are in trouble again.
Thus they take away our ability to predict the future. We are crippled. Because the countless paths followed to reach desired results are not grounded in logic. Their foundations are subjective interpretations of the past. Unless we detach our identity from them and extract ourselves from this cesspool, our existence can never attain an individual dimension.
Even if you observe, even if you know and foresee, even if you hold a piece of paper stating what will happen in the future, you can do nothing. This is a defense mechanism created by society to protect its own interests. It has shaped itself so that thoughts outside the system are terminated before they begin.
This is why artists and works that were not understood in their time gain value later. Even if such attempts are initially suppressed, the spirit of the age—zeitgeist—eventually generates numerous repetitions. The system is forced to assimilate them as part of itself. The church that once burned scientists for saying the Earth was round later elects a pope who says, “Of course there is a Big Bang; did you think God was a magician?” The heretics of their time are declared saints thousands of years after their deaths.

As if there were another way.
Miyamoto Musashi was a ronin once described to me as quite famous in history. This man won 62 recorded duels in his lifetime. These were duels to the death with swords. A single mistake could cost your life. Yet Musashi did not die in combat; he died of old age.
In his first duel, at age 13, he defeated an adult samurai armed with a sword using only a stick. In most of his fights, he used a simple stick against sword-bearing opponents. His methods were described as brutal, far from the elegance associated with samurai.
His mission was to expose impostors who declared themselves samurai and spoke of the “true way” while remaining untouchable due to status. He tested whether what they preached in their dojos was true, and the best way to prove it was through a duel.
Shortly before his death, Musashi wrote a small collection of 21 principles distilled from his life. He named his path “The Path of Solitude.” In a world of deceivers, solitude becomes inevitable for the honest.
Similar words are attributed to Nikola Tesla:
"Be alone, that is the secret of invention; be alone, that is when ideas are born" - Nikola Tesla
Today, success stories focus solely on results. Figures like Steve Jobs claim that no one can foresee the future, only connect the dots afterward. Yet foresight is possible. Humans think when confronted with problems. History and evolution demonstrate this.
Homo erectus and Neanderthals remained within temperate climates and rarely ventured far. Homo sapiens, by contrast, continually overcame obstacles. Ecological disasters do not necessarily bring apocalypse; they become new barriers to surpass.

Other dogs bite their enemies; I bite my friends—to save them.
If you can foresee what may happen, then play your role. Do not fear risk or loss. Let yourself be hurt. Let yourself be alone. Human existence is inseparable from suffering; the promise of peace is a construct meant to numb us.
Those who truly see the future are the ones who can change things. Perhaps you can be one of them.
Just take part in breaking this machine so that it malfunctions and is forced to change.
